title: Microburst mitigation: pacing and placement playbook for multi-GPU LLM inference
content:
Summary:

This is a working playbook capturing experiments and heuristics for mitigating microburst-driven tail-latency and cross-GPU congestion in multi‑GPU LLM inference. Focus is on inference workloads (small batches, streaming token emission) where per-request bursts of NVLink/PCIe/NCCL traffic create transient backpressure, head-of-line blocking, and sometimes kernel serialization on adjacent GPUs.

Why this matters:
- Customer use-cases: streaming chat, low-latency token-by-token generation, interactive apps (PLG flows).
- Symptoms we see: sporadic 2–10x tail latency spikes, NCCL stalls in traces, imbalanced link utilization, and worse p99 when many concurrent small requests share a node.

High-level hypotheses (tested in doc):
1) Microbursts arise when many small messages (KV cache updates, attention KV transfers, small tensor allreduces) are emitted synchronously across workers.
2) NCCL eager/rendezvous thresholds and the RDMA transport can amplify microbursts (small messages get sent immediately, causing switch/queue pressure).
3) Co-placement of tensor/pipeline peers on same NVSwitch island vs cross-node matters: intra-island placement reduces wire hops but concentrates bursts; spreading can reduce instantaneous contention at cost of latency.
4) Simple runtime pacing (per-token spacing or tiny batching) reduces tail latency more effectively than heavyweight kernel changes.

Platform / software baseline used for experiments:
- Servers: 8x A100 80GB per node, NVSwitch, PCIe Gen4 CPU interconnect; also small run on 4xH100 node for cross-check.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04; CUDA 12.2; NVIDIA driver 535.x; NCCL 2.18; ibverbs + UCX stack for RDMA tests.
- Runtime: Redwood serving-runtime branch: feature/pacing-v1 (PR 1783).
- Models: 6.9B decoder-only (sequence len 2048), 33B conversational test model (sharded tensor-parallel + pipeline stages).

Experiment matrix (short):
- Placement: co-locate pipeline neighbors on same NVSwitch vs spread across switches vs cross-node.
- NCCL transport: TCP vs IB (RDMA) vs NVLink; adjust NCCL_P2P_DISABLE, NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME for controlled runs.
- Message size profiles: force many small messages (8–64KB) vs aggregated large (several MB).
- Pacing: none, fixed inter-token gap (0.5–4ms), token aggregation (group N tokens before KV flush), adaptive token pacing (leaky bucket).
- Concurrency: 1, 8, 32 concurrent streams.

Key commands and profiling snippets (working notes):
- NCCL/env tuning snapshot: 
  export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO
  export NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0
  export NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0
  export NCCL_BUFFSIZE=1048576
  export NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=PARALLEL
- System tracing: nsys profile --output=run1 --trace=cuda,cublas,nvtx,nccl --sample=none 
- Kernel-level: nvprof / Nsight to capture kernel queues and timelines (nsys timeline used for visualization).
- Network capture: ibv_devinfo; iblinkinfo for IB counters; nvidia-smi topo -m for topology.

Observed signals (representative):
- Trace: synchronized spikes in NCCL allreduce start times across ranks, then a long wait (200–800us) for some ranks -> corresponds to NIC queue flushing.
- Bandwidth: short periods (200–600us) at >200GB/s aggregated on NVSwitch lanes, then near-zero, then burst again.
- Kernel queuing: concurrent kernels on GPUs becoming serialized because memcpy/cross-device copy monopolizes DMA engines.
- CPU metrics: per-CPU soft IRQ spikes on IB devices during microbursts.

Quantitative example (33B model, 8-concurrency, default/no-pacing):
- median per-token latency: 28ms
- p95: 45ms
- p99: 180ms (heavy tail caused by microbursts)
After enabling simple fixed pacing (0.8ms inter-token):
- median: 30ms (slightly higher)
- p95: 34ms
- p99: 52ms
Notes: slight median increase but dramatic p99 reduction, throughput loss ~6–9% depending on sequence length.

What we tried and outcome (short log):
- NCCL_BUFFSIZE increase -> small improvement in throughput variance but not tail. Hypothesis: reduces number of NCCL messages but not alignment with bursts.
- Switch to IB/RDMA -> sometimes reduced CPU pressure but increased sporadic tail when network driver rate-limited.
- Kernel-level merging (aggregate KV writes) -> reduces message count; requires changes in runtime memory management; effective but invasive.
- Staggered scheduling across pipeline stages (random jitter 0–1ms) -> similar effect to pacing with lower throughput loss.
- NIC offload and GDR tweaks -> helpful on H100, inconsistent on older NIC stacks.

Practical mitigations and heuristics for runtime (actionable):
1) Soft pacing leaky-bucket per-request: track last-send timestamp, ensure minimum inter-send gap (configurable by model size and batch). Default 0.5–1.0ms for large models.
2) Opportunistic tiny-aggregation: hold tiny KV updates for up to X tokens or Y microseconds then flush (trade-off: memory vs. fewer messages).
3) Placement hints: prefer placing tensors so that heavy allreduce partners share NVSwitch island OR conversely spread when expected concurrency high. Make placement policy configurable per-customer.
4) Adaptive mode: when node-level queue length (NIC/IB/driver metrics) hits threshold, increase pacing/jitter or switch transport fallback.
5) NCCL envs: enforce LAUNCH_MODE=PARALLEL and tune NCCL_BUFFSIZE to encourage fewer messages for the given model profile. Document per-hardware defaults.
6) Monitoring: add NVSwitch utilization histogram, per-link microburst counters, and incorporate into console alerting (p99 drift + link-burst rate).

Runtime instrumentation to add (low-effort):
- Per-request NVTX zones for all communication ops (KV read/write, attention allreduce, gather/scatter) so traces correlate network activity with token timing.
- Emit small heartbeat metrics: last_send_ms, queued_messages, avg_message_sz, pacer_delay.
- Expose NCCL queue depth approximations via runtime counters (best-effort).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Best placement heuristic when mixing short/long requests? E.g., co-locate pipeline stages for long-running sessions but spread for many short chat sessions.
- Can smart batching at the RDMA level (driver/UCX) be used to coalesce messages without runtime changes? Ask infra/ucx team.
- Explore hardware pacing: programmable NICs that can smooth bursts without CPU involvement.
- Formalize trade-off curve: throughput vs p99 for each workload class and present to product for default config recommendations.

Immediate next steps (owner assignments):
- Ayesha: implement per-request leaky-bucket pacing (prototype merged in feature/pacing-v1).
- Liam: add NVTX zones + nsys dashboards for the nightly perf job. (JIRA-RT-8421)
- Marcos: run placement sweeps across more hardware (H100 + older NVSwitch) and dump full traces.
- Evelyn: draft doc for Console metrics + alerts for microburst detection.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Need small synthetic workload generator that reproduces microburst signature reliably (script: synthetic/microburst/repro.sh).
- Keep pacing on by default for hosted API but allow enterprise Dedicated customers to opt-out with rationale.
- If we expose pacing knobs via API, provide safety guards to avoid accidental throughput collapse.

Appendix: useful commands / snippets
- nsys recording: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,nccl --output=trace-run-$(date +%s) ./serving-runtime --profile-mode
- quick NCCL info: python -c 'import nccl; print(nccl.get_version())' (runtime wrapper)
- ib counters: sudo ethtool -S mlx5_core | egrep "tx|rx|drop"

References / links:
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1783 (pacing prototype)
- JIRA: JIRA-RT-8421 (end-to-end profiling job)
- External: UCX knobs primer (link internal), NVIDIA microburst note (internal link)

End of draft. Will convert to a more prescriptive playbook after additional runs and when the placement sweep completes.
notes: informal working doc: expect edits, more traces to be uploaded to the perf bucket. priority: reduce p99 for hosted chat flows.
